title: Revelation comes to the mind and heart by the Holy Ghost
setting: Oliver Cowdery began writing for Joseph Smith at Harmony, Pennsylvania, in April 1829. An earlier revelation, now section 6, had offered him a gift to translate. Oliver wanted that power, and this revelation answered his request. In the earliest copy, his second gift is called working with the “sprout,” or rod. Many people then used such rods to search for water or minerals. Later editions call it the gift of Aaron.
summary: The revelation promises Oliver Cowdery knowledge of whatever he asks in faith with an honest heart. It applies this to the engravings of ancient records. It says the Lord will speak to his mind and heart by the Holy Ghost. It calls this the spirit of revelation, the spirit by which Moses led Israel through the Red Sea. It names a second gift, the gift of Aaron, which only God’s power can make work. It warns that without faith he can do nothing and should not ask for what he ought not. It invites him to ask to know mysteries and to translate sacred records.

contextNote.title: Where the answer arrives
contextNote.text: Oliver wanted to know how translation would work for him. Verse 2 says the Lord will speak “in your mind and in your heart” by the Holy Ghost. Verse 3 calls this “the spirit of revelation” and ties it to the spirit by which Moses brought Israel through the Red Sea. Verse 1 sets the conditions: asking in faith, with an honest heart. Verse 10 repeats that without faith he can do nothing. In this section, revelation is knowledge that reaches thought and feeling together.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 6–9 teaches that Heavenly Father speaks to us through the Holy Ghost. Why might verse 2 name both mind and heart, and how does verse 3 connect that to Moses?
reviewNote: Read all 12 verses. Official heading gives Harmony, April 1829, through Joseph Smith to Oliver Cowdery, who asked for the gift of translation. JSP historical introduction read for the link to D&C 6 and the earliest wording “the gift of working with the sprout,” likely divining-rod use; the claim that later editions read “gift of Aaron” is from the current text and general knowledge of the 1835 revision. Aaron is not added as a person since the name labels the gift. Fact-check 2026-10-12: contextNote no longer says the spirit "parted" the Red Sea (verse 3 says Moses brought Israel through it); summary now attributes the Holy Ghost promise to the text.
